title: `proc_get_status()` now returns the right value on every call, not just the first
summary: As of PHP 8.3, calling proc_get_status() more than once on the same process handle always returns the correct running/exitcode/signaled state on POSIX systems, and proc_close() called afterward now also returns the real exit code instead of -1; UPGRADING states that previously only the first call returned the right value. This rule documents a bug fix, not a regression: below 8.3, code had to capture the first call's result and reuse it; from 8.3 it can call freely, and a new "cached" array key reports whether a given result came from that internal cache.
new_code_policy: On a PHP 8.3+ floor, it is safe to call proc_get_status() as many times as you need - in a polling loop, from multiple places in the code, however the logic is structured - and trust each call's own return value directly: verified directly, running, exitcode, signaled, and the rest are correct on every call, not only the first, on POSIX systems, and proc_close() called after any number of proc_get_status() calls still returns the process's real exit code rather than -1. There is no need to defensively capture-and-reuse the first call's array purely to work around unreliable later calls; that workaround is no longer necessary here. If the project's floor still includes anything below 8.3 (a range-safe policy spanning 8.2-8.5, for example), keep writing the defensive capture-once pattern anyway, since it is exactly as correct on 8.3+ as calling repeatedly is - just no longer the only correct option - while remaining required below 8.3. A new "cached" key in the returned array reports whether that specific result came from the internal cache (true once the process has exited and its status is being served from the stored record) versus a live check (false, seen while the process is still running); it is informational, not something you must inspect to get a correct result on 8.3+.
existing_code_policy: Find every proc_get_status() call site and determine which of two shapes it already has. (1) The defensive shape: the code calls proc_get_status() once, immediately after believing the process may have exited, stores that single returned array, and reuses the stored array (not a fresh call) for every later decision, including whatever exit code it reports to its own caller. This shape needs no change - verified directly, it continues to work correctly on 8.3+, and per UPGRADING's own wording it was already the only reliable shape on any version before 8.3, since "only the first call to that function would return the right value" there. (2) The repeated-call shape: the code calls proc_get_status() more than once and trusts each call's own return value independently - for example, a polling loop that re-reads $status['running'] or $status['exitcode'] fresh on every iteration, or two different code paths that each call it separately. Audit the project's actual PHP floor before deciding this is fine: on a PHP 8.3+-only floor it is fine, and per UPGRADING was in fact a latent bug on any earlier version, silently capable of reporting a stale or wrong running/exitcode/signaled value after the first call; on a floor that still includes 8.2, this shape must be rewritten to the defensive capture-once pattern (or the code must branch on PHP_VERSION_ID), because a second or later call there is not guaranteed correct. Separately, audit any call site that invokes proc_close() after having called proc_get_status() at all: per UPGRADING, before 8.3 this combination could make proc_close() itself return -1 instead of the process's real exit code, so code on a pre-8.3 floor that needs a trustworthy exit code from proc_close() specifically must not have called proc_get_status() first on that same handle - get the exit code from the first (and only trusted) proc_get_status() call instead, and do not also rely on proc_close()'s return value there. Do not "clean up" an existing capture-once pattern into free repeated calls without first confirming the project's supported floor is 8.3+, since doing so would reintroduce, on any lower floor still in scope, precisely the bug this PHP version fixed.
guideline: Below a PHP 8.3 floor, call proc_get_status() once, store its result, and make every later decision from that stored value - a second live call, and calling proc_close() after any proc_get_status() call, are not guaranteed correct there. From PHP 8.3, this is a fixed bug: proc_get_status() can be called as many times as needed and each call reports the process's true current state, and proc_close() afterward reports the real exit code; the array's new "cached" key tells you whether a given result came from the stored record (process already exited) or a live check (process still running), but you do not need to consult it to get a correct answer.
details:
UPGRADING-8.3.0 lists this under Backward Incompatible Changes -> Core: "Executing proc_get_status() multiple times will now always return the right value on posix systems. Previously, only the first call to that function returned the right value. Executing proc_close() after proc_get_status() will now also return the right exit code. Previously this would return -1. Internally, this works by caching the result on posix systems. If you want the old behaviour, you can check the 'cached' key in the array returned by proc_get_status() to check whether the result was cached." This describes two related pre-8.3 failure modes together, neither of which this tool can observe firsthand - the local host is PHP 8.4.19, already fixed, and no earlier PHP was available to run here - so both are reported from UPGRADING's own wording, not from a runtime measurement: (a) a second or later proc_get_status() call on the same handle was not guaranteed to report the process's actual running/exitcode state, only the first call was; (b) calling proc_close() on a handle that had already had proc_get_status() called on it could itself return -1 in place of the process's real exit code, rather than only the repeated proc_get_status() calls being affected.

The fix, and the "cached" key, were verified directly on PHP 8.4.19. Using proc_open() to run a short-lived child process (sh -c "sleep 0.2; exit 7") and polling proc_get_status() on the same handle roughly every 50ms: while the child was still running, every call returned running=true, exitcode=-1, cached=false; the moment the child was first observed to have exited, that call and every call afterward (six further polls, well past the transition) returned running=false, exitcode=7, cached=true - the correct exit code, held stable across repeated calls, not just reported once and then lost or corrupted. proc_close() called at the end returned 7, the process's real exit code, confirming the second half of UPGRADING's text directly: calling it after multiple prior proc_get_status() calls did not produce -1. A second fixture (sh -c "exit 42", given time to exit before any status call) confirmed the same pattern with a different exit code: three consecutive proc_get_status() calls each returned running=false, exitcode=42, cached=true, and the subsequent proc_close() returned 42.

What "cached" actually distinguishes, per this measurement, is a live check versus a captured snapshot, not strictly "first call versus later calls": every call observed while the process was still running reported cached=false (a fresh check each time), and every call observed once the process had exited reported cached=true, including the very first call that detected the exit - there was no observed moment where the exit was freshly detected with cached=false and only became true on a subsequent call. This is consistent with UPGRADING's own description of the mechanism ("this works by caching the result... on posix systems"): once PHP has successfully reaped the child's exit status once, it stores that result rather than attempting to wait on the (now-reaped, and on POSIX no longer waitable) process again, and reports every later read - including, apparently, the one that performed the reap - as coming from that stored record.

Here introduced_in is set to 8.3 because that is the minor this fix actually landed in - the field exists so this behavior_change rule can be range-gated on the feature axis, and it is not a claim that PHP 8.3 introduced proc_open()/proc_get_status()/proc_close() themselves, which have existed since PHP's earliest versions. Because this rule documents a correctness fix rather than a new restriction, its guidance runs in the opposite direction from most other rules this catalog tracks: the burden falls on code that must still support a floor below 8.3, not on code that has already moved past it.

before: // A second call, made after the loop above already called it repeatedly:
after: // Reuse the status array from the call that actually observed the exit,
// rather than calling proc_get_status() again, so this stays correct
// on a floor that still includes PHP 8.2.

before: // Called from a separate method than isRunning(), so this is
// whichever numbered call happens to land here at runtime.
after: // Capture the call that first observes the exit, and reuse it -
// correct on every PHP version this catalog tracks, not only 8.3+.
return $this->finalStatus['exitcode'] ?? throw new LogicException('Process has not exited yet');

notes: Runtime matrix executed on PHP 8.4.19 (2026-09-06), PHP_OS_FAMILY=Linux. Fixture 1 (sh -c "sleep 0.2; exit 7", polled every ~50ms): while running, every poll returned running=true exitcode=-1 cached=false; from the first poll that observed the exit through six further polls, every one returned running=false exitcode=7 cached=true; proc_close() afterward returned 7. Fixture 2 (sh -c "exit 42", given 300ms to exit before any call): three consecutive proc_get_status() calls each returned running=false exitcode=42 signaled=false stopped=false cached=true; proc_close() afterward returned 42. Both fixtures confirm every one of several repeated calls agreed with each other and with the correct exit code, and that proc_close() after multiple proc_get_status() calls returned the real exit code rather than -1.

The pre-8.3 failure mode itself - "only the first call... returned the right value" and proc_close() returning -1 after a proc_get_status() call - is reported from UPGRADING-8.3.0's own text only, not from a runtime observation: this host is PHP 8.4.19, already fixed, and no earlier PHP was available to run here, so the old, broken behavior could not be executed or confirmed directly.

PHPCompatibility 10.0.0-alpha2 was run directly (2026-09-06) via `phpcs --standard=PHPCompatibility --runtime-set testVersion 8.2-8.5 --report=json --parallel=1 --extensions=php --severity=1 --no-cache -q` against a class that opens a process, calls proc_get_status() twice, and calls proc_close(), at testVersion 8.2-8.5, and produced zero findings ({"errors":0,"warnings":0,"fixable":0}); verification.phpcompatibility is intentionally empty rather than guessed. This is the structural blindness described in the round's shared contract: PHPCompatibility checks version availability of functions and syntax, not that a function's return value became reliable across repeated calls, so a clean phpcs run gives no signal about this behavior at all.

Evidence: UPGRADING-8.3.0, "1. Backward Incompatible Changes" -> Core: "Executing proc_get_status() multiple times will now always return the right value on posix systems. Previously, only the first call of the function returned the right value. Executing proc_close() after proc_get_status() will now also return the right exit code. Previously this would return -1. Internally, this works by caching the result on posix systems. If you want the old behaviour, you can check the 'cached' key in the array returned by proc_get_status() to check whether the result was cached." Grepping the PHP 8.4 and 8.5 UPGRADING files for "proc_get_status", "proc_close", and "proc_open" found no matches, so this behavior persists unchanged through PHP 8.5.
